“Then, taking the tray of this prasada on her lap, she burst into tears, thinking: ‘My beloved son Nimai loves all these dishes so much. But Nimai is not here. Who will eat all this?’ Thinking of Me with such great love, she shed bitter tears. At once I came and ate all these dishes. Seeing the empty tray, she was astonished and wiped away her tears.” (CC, Madhya 15.56–58)

“Who has eaten it? Could it be Bala-Gopala Himself? Or was I only imagining it?” she wondered, and finding the pots in the kitchen full, she called Ishana to clean up and prepared a new offering for Gopala; and the Lord, summoned by her love, again ate it all. “Ask her about it,” He told Srivasa, “and confirm that she did not imagine anything” (15.59–66).

Srivasa and his brothers, having moved to Kumarahatta, went every year both to the Lord in Nilachala and to Shachi in Mayapur, and then stayed for several days in their house in Navadvipa. “In Bengal I have two merciful refuges — My mother and the Ganga,” the Lord would say (CC, Madhya 16.90), and Gadadhara Pandita, not wishing to let Him go alone, said, “I am going not for Your sake, but to see mother Shachi” (16.135).

Five Years Later

Five years after His sannyasa, in 1514, the Lord Himself came to Bengal — to see His mother and the Ganga. For seven days He stayed in Kulia, in the house of Madhava Dasa (CC, Madhya 16.208–209), Vamshivadana's father, and there bestowed His mercy on Devananda Pandita; then He visited Ramakeli and came to Shantipur, to Advaita's house. Having received the Lord of His life in His own home, Advaita was beside Himself with happiness, and when He had calmed a little, He sent people to Navadvipa with a palanquin for mother Shachi (CB, Antya 4.209–212).23

Vrindavana Dasa describes the state in which the messengers found her. Through five years of separation Yashoda had come to light in her ever more fully:

“Sometimes mother Shachi would cry out: ‘Rama! Krishna! Go quickly and milk the cows. I am going to sell milk.’ Sometimes mother Shachi ran about with a stick in her hand, saying: ‘Catch Him! Catch Him! Where is that butter thief? You won't escape! Today I shall tie You up.’ Saying this, she ran about in bliss.” (CB, Antya 4.218–220)

She asked everyone about Mathura — what Krishna and Balarama were doing there, what had become of Kamsa — scolded “the thief Akrura” who had stolen her sons, called on someone to come and bathe in the Yamuna; she wept so that stones cracked, laughed for six hours at a time seeing Krishna in meditation, lay for three hours without a sign of life (4.213–227). And Vrindavana Dasa explains:

“Mother Shachi's ecstatic love cannot be compared with anything. She alone displayed such boundless love. Gaurachandra endowed mother Shachi with the same potency of loving service to Krishna that He Himself possessed.” (CB, Antya 4.228–229)

And whenever she came to outer consciousness, it was only to serve Vishnu (4.232).

The news, “Gaurasundara is in Shantipur,” filled her with indescribable happiness. Gangadasa Pandita set out with her at once, and Murari Gupta and other devotees joined them.24 As soon as the Lord saw His mother, He fell prostrate before her, walked around her again and again and, weeping with happiness, prayed to her:

“‘You are the Mother of the universe and the embodiment of loving service to God. Your form is wholly spiritual and transcendent to the gunas of material nature. As soon as you cast a merciful glance on living beings, attraction to Krishna awakens in them. You are the embodiment of loving service to Vishnu. You are the divine power that gives rise to everything. You are the Ganga, Devaki, Yashoda, Devahuti, Prishni, Anasuya, Kaushalya and Aditi. All that you see comes from you. You are the keeper of all, and all at last finds rest in you. Who can tell of your greatness? You dwell in the heart of everyone.’” (CB, Antya 4.242–247)

“The Lord said: ‘The devotion to Krishna that I possess has come to Me only by your mercy. Millions of servants of your servants are dearer to Me than My own life. Even one who remembers you but once will never again fall into the cycle of birth and death. The Ganga and tulasi purify all they touch. But even they are purified by your touch. I am unable to repay you for the love you showed in caring for Me.’” (CB, Antya 4.253–257)

Shachi, seeing her son's face, stood still in ecstasy. She knew that her son was Narayana Himself and could say whatever He wished, and on coming to herself she answered:

“After a few moments mother Shachi said: ‘Is anyone able to understand Your words? Conditioned souls are like lifeless bodies tossed from side to side by the waves of the ocean. All living beings are in the ocean of material existence, wholly in the power of Your illusory energy. My dear son, I can only say that You alone know what the true good of each one is. You may offer prayers, make obeisances and reverently walk around, for I know that You always act as You please.’” (CB, Antya 4.261–265)

The devotees cried out, “Jaya! Jaya!” The mother's happiness made Nityananda mad with ecstasy, and Advaita bowed to her without end, reciting the prayers with which Devaki is glorified (4.266–272).

Advaita asked the Lord to allow Shachi to cook. She cooked with great joy, thinking, “Gaurachandra is Narayana Himself.” Knowing that her son loved shak, she prepared twenty kinds of it, and every dish in ten or twenty variations, and laid out the rice and vegetables in rows, adorning them with tulasi blossoms. Entering, the Lord prostrated Himself before this meal: “The mere sight of these dishes frees one from the bonds of material life… I think Krishna Himself with His companions has tasted this feast.” He ate, praising each kind of shak, while His mother watched, “wishing to give full satisfaction to her eyes” (CB, Antya 4.276–299); afterwards the devotees, playfully quarrelling, shared out the remnants of His meal (4.305–313). During that same visit Advaita held a festival on the day of worship (aradhana) of His guru Madhavendra Puri, and again “Ai” volunteered to cook, while the wives of the Vaishnavas helped her; the Lord and all the devotees partook of her cooking (CB, Antya 4.441–447, 506). Murari Gupta says that the Lord, “the crest-jewel of those devoted to their mothers”, had her brought from Navadvipa, dispelled her grief and ate the food she had cooked (“Kadacha” 3.18.19–20). He also tells how the Lord, coming from Kulia to Navadvipa, fell at His mother's feet, and she hastily embraced Him and, having fed Him food of the four kinds, “the loving mother was filled with joy” (4.14.4–5), and how Gaura and Nitai, having spent several days with Advaita, “obedient to Their mother's will”, gladdened her with sweet words and left (4.15.6–12).25

Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of this visit briefly: in Shantipur the Lord met His mother and consoled her, freeing her from all sorrow, and then, returning from Ramakeli, stayed with Advaita for ten days (CC, Madhya 16.210–212).26 Seeing her son after a long separation, Shachi utterly forgot herself and for many days cooked for Him. And at the farewell the Lord

“humbly fell at His mother's feet and received her permission to set out on the path to Vraja-dhama.” (CC, Madhya 16.249)

Mother Shachi was escorted back to Navadvipa, and the Lord returned to Nilachala (16.250).

Nityananda with Shachi

The Lord sent Nityananda to preach in Bengal, and He, going from village to village, one day felt a desire to see mother Shachi (CB, Antya 5.421). Coming to Navadvipa, He went first of all to her house and bowed at her feet:

“Mother Shachi said: ‘My dear son. Surely You are the Supersoul of all creation, for I have been able to see You as soon as I wished it. Knowing my desire, You appeared here at once. So who in this world can understand You? My dear son, stay in Navadvipa for a little while, so that I may see You every ten, fifteen or thirty days.’” (CB, Antya 5.499–501)

“O mother of all that exists, I have come here to see you,” answered Nityananda, “and with your permission I shall stay in Navadvipa” (5.504–505). Murari Gupta tells of this meeting thus: “Mother, I have come, and I am happy!” said Nityananda, and she, placing her hands on His head, begged, “Stay in my house, so that I may always see You.” He replied with a smile:

“‘Mother, listen, I will tell you the truth: I and My younger brother always live beside you, always close to you. The food you cook is filled with the nectar of Sri Krishna's lips — it is out of longing for it, Mother, that I always stay near you.’” (“Kadacha” 4.23.4–5)

And when she served the meal, she saw that it was Rama and Krishna who were eating it, and was plunged in an ocean of joy (4.23.6–8).

After His marriage Nityananda brought His wives, Vasudha and Jahnava, to her; Shachi welcomed them with great joy, would not let them out of her embrace and tenderly caressed them both. At her wish Nityananda then lived nearby for some time before settling in Khardaha.27 And when separation from Gaura became unbearable, He would ask Shachi's permission and go back to Nilachala (CB, Antya 7.10–11).

Damodara Pandita and Jagadananda

The most impartial of His companions, Damodara Pandita, the Lord sent to live with His mother:

“Apart from you I see no one who could look after her and protect her. You have surrounded even Me with your care.” (CC, Antya 3.22)

“Go to My mother's house and take shelter at her holy feet. In your presence no one will dare to behave as he pleases.” (CC, Antya 3.25)

Damodara was told to bow to her again and again on her son's behalf, to tell her how well He was, and to remind her of one secret:

“Tell her: ‘O My dear mother! Again and again I come to your house and eat all the sweets and vegetable dishes that you offer Me…’” (CC, Antya 3.30)

On the last Magha-sankranti, the Lord went on, she had prepared various dishes, cakes, sweet rice and condensed milk, offered them to Krishna and sat down to meditate. Suddenly He came and hastily ate it all, and her eyes filled with tears of joy; but when she had wiped them she saw the empty tray and decided that she had dreamt it. Then, in the confusion of separation, she thought that she had not made the offering at all, went to the kitchen, found the pots full, cleaned the place and offered again (3.32–37).

“Thus again and again I ate all the offerings you made Me, attracted by your pure love. I live in Jagannatha Puri only in obedience to your instruction. Yet the power of your pure love draws Me so irresistibly that I am unable to resist.” (CC, Antya 3.38–39)

Damodara brought her Jagannatha's prasada — for her and for the devotees of Navadvipa — and stayed to live at her feet (3.40–42).

Once, when Damodara had visited Shachi and returned to Nilachala, the Lord called him aside and asked, “You have been staying with My mother. Tell Me the truth: is she devoted to Lord Vishnu?” The stern Damodara answered in anger:

“‘O Gosvami, what are You saying? You ask whether Your mother has devotion to God? Your devotion to Lord Vishnu has come to You by the mercy of Your mother. All that You have has come through her. Know that all the devotion You have has come to You by her mercy. On mother Shachi's body one can always see such signs of divine love for Vishnu as weeping, trembling, perspiration, fainting, hair standing on end and loud cries. She constantly chants the holy name of Krishna. O Gosvami, You ask about mother Shachi's devotion? Is it not mother Shachi who is addressed as Vishnu-bhakti, loving devotion to Vishnu?’” (CB, Antya 9.95–100)

The Lord's happiness knew no bounds. He embraced Damodara:

“‘O Damodara, today you have bought Me, fully confirming the feeling of My heart. All the devotion to Vishnu that I possess has come to Me by the mercy of My mother. Of this there is no doubt. By her will I live in this world. Therefore I can never repay her for it. O Damodara, please hear Me. I am wholly conquered by her love. I always see her.’” (CB, Antya 9.105–108)

He asked, says Vrindavana Dasa, only to instruct the world (9.110). Murari Gupta gives the same conversation: “It is only by her grace that there is in You that devotion,” Damodara answered angrily, and the Lord said, “It is only by her command that I live in this Kshetra — and yet her love draws Me back to her again and again” (“Kadacha” 4.20.1–4).

Every year the Lord sent Jagadananda to His mother as well. He bowed at her feet on the Lord's behalf, gave her cloth and Jagannatha's prasada, conveyed the Lord's humble prayers, and she listened day and night to his tales of her son. “Sometimes,” Jagadananda told her, “Chaitanya comes to you and eats, and afterwards says, ‘Today Mother has fed Me to the full,’” and Shachi confessed:

“Shachimata said: ‘How I wish that Nimai would eat all these dishes that I cook from the finest vegetables. Sometimes it seems to me that Nimai has eaten all the food on the tray, but afterwards I take it for a dream.’” (CC, Antya 12.93–94)

One biography adds that Jagadananda, naming the exact days, confirmed to her that her son had come in reality, and she believed that it was no dream.28 Next to her house lived the confectioner Parameshvara, who also went to Puri with the pilgrims from Bengal (12.54).

Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls the Lord “the crown of all who are devoted to their mother” and gives His words, which Jagadananda carried to Nadia every year:

“‘Go to Nadia and convey My obeisances to My mother. On My behalf touch her lotus feet. Tell her: “Remember, every day I come and bow at your feet. Whenever you wish to feed Me, I surely come and eat all that you offer. I abandoned service to you and took sannyasa. I became a madman and neglected My duty. Do not hold this offence against Me. I am in your power — for I am your son. I live in Nilachala at your command and, as long as I live, I cannot leave this place.”’” (CC, Antya 19.6–11)

The prasada-cloth from the festival of Jagannatha's cowherd pastimes the Lord, on the advice of Paramananda Puri, sent to His mother, and the best prasada He collected separately for her and the devotees (19.12–13):

“Mahaprabhu is the crown of all who are devoted to their mother. Even after taking sannyasa, He always served her.” (CC, Antya 19.14)

After staying a month in Nadia, Jagadananda returned to Puri with her permission (19.15–16). In sending His mother Jagannatha's prasada, the sannyasi Lord showed not worldly attachment but transcendental love for His eternal companions — and His mother is the first of them. Nor did He ever leave her:

“The Lord is always attracted by divine love, for such is His nature. Therefore Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu always manifested Himself in four places: in mother Shachi's home temple, in the place where Nityananda Prabhu dances, in the kirtana of Srivasa Thakura and in the house of Raghava Pandita.” (CC, Antya 2.34–35)

Departure and Remembrance

When Shachi Devi hid herself from the eyes of this world the original sources do not say; the days of her appearance and departure are not in the Vaishnava calendar either. Ishana and Vamshivadana — the servants and protectors of Shachi and Vishnupriya — were with her to the end; every morning Vishnupriya went with her to bathe in the Ganga and ate only the remnants of her food; and their affairs, according to one biography, were also managed by Gadadhara Dasa, who, when they were gone, moved to Katva. All that is known is that after the departure of Mahaprabhu and Shachi Vamshivadana served Vishnupriya and the aged Ishana, and that Jahnava, coming to the Lord's house in Navadvipa after the festival at Kheturi, no longer found Shachi there and grieved that she had missed her. To Srinivasa Acharya, who came to Navadvipa to the Lord's family, mother Shachi showed mercy, “appearing as if in a dream” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.55).29

Her memory is kept by songs. Vasudeva Ghosha sings of the Boy who circles about Shachi's courtyard, hides and teases His mother, and when she calls, “Vishvambhara, where are You?” runs to her and catches the hem of her sari. And Narottama Dasa sums it up: the son of the king of Vraja has become the son of Shachi, and Balarama has become Nitai. When the Lord's birthplace was rediscovered at the end of the nineteenth century, Jagannatha Dasa Babaji proposed that the Deities of Jagannatha and Shachi be worshipped there in one temple, and Mahaprabhu with Lakshmipriya and Vishnupriya in another.

Queen of Vraja

Who, then, was this brahmana woman of Navadvipa, a widow who lost eight daughters and her husband and let two sons go into sannyasa? The original sources answer with one voice: the Mother of the universe, Yashoda, service to Vishnu embodied. In her arms wept He whom time and death fear; her cooking was eaten by Him, coming secretly from Nilachala, for whose sake sages fast; her permission was asked, on leaving, by Him who depends on no one. Only His eternal companion can treat the Lord as a son, and the whole of Shachi's life — from the lullaby to the twelve-day fast — is vatsalya, pure motherly love, in which the Lord's majesty is not forgotten but dissolved. The Lord Himself told her, “Nothing will ever separate you and Me”; and He still appears in her house, for where He is loved so, He cannot but be.
